title: Kailash Yatra Rules for Indian Passport Holders
meta_description: Kailash yatra rules for Indian passport holders via Nepal: group visa through New Delhi, biometrics, age limit, NRI groups, documents. Check current status.
summary: Indian citizens can do the Kailash yatra via Nepal with a Chinese group visa and Tibet permits arranged by a licensed agency. In recent seasons resident Indians have applied through New Delhi with original passports weeks ahead, completed biometrics and met an age limit near 70. These rules have changed several times since 2023; check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: The short version
paras: There are two ways for an Indian citizen to reach Kailash. The first is the Government of India's Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, run by the Ministry of External Affairs via the Lipulekh pass and Nathu La, with a computerised draw. The second is a private yatra through Nepal, arranged by a Nepali agency working with a licensed Tibetan agency, via Kyirong, Hilsa or Lhasa. This guide covers the Nepal routes.

On the Nepal routes, the essentials have stayed the same: you travel in a group on a Chinese group visa, with a Tibet Travel Permit and area permits obtained by the Tibetan agency, and you cannot travel independently in Tibet. What has changed, sometimes from one season to the next, is where the visa is processed, how long it takes, whether biometrics are needed, which fees apply, the age limit and how non-resident Indians are grouped. Everything below reflects our understanding at the time of writing. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: What has changed since 2023
paras: Tibet was closed to foreign pilgrims from 2020 until 2023. When Kailash reopened through Nepal, Indian nationals found a different process from before the pandemic, and the rules have been adjusted in most seasons since. Nepal-based operators have reported the following changes at various points; not all have applied in every year.
list: Visa processing for resident Indians moved to the Chinese embassy in New Delhi, with original passports submitted about a month before departure
Group visa processing times extended, reported at about six working days in the 2026 season
Biometric data collection added for pilgrims, at the embassy or in Kathmandu
A dual submission system requiring both online forms and physical documents
Non-resident Indians required to form separate groups of at least five with other NRIs or foreign nationals
An age limit around 70, expressed for 2026 as birth year 1955 or later, with conditional exceptions reported in some seasons
Fees and service charges specific to Indian nationals in some seasons
Border disruption: Rasuwagadhi–Kyirong closed by floods from July 2025 to January 2026 and again from 26 August 2026

sections.heading: Documents Indian pilgrims need
paras: Prepare these well before booking. Agencies submit them to the Tibetan partner, who applies for permits, and to the embassy for the group visa. Keep several photocopies and scans.
list: Indian passport valid for at least six months beyond the trip, with at least two blank pages
Clear colour scan of the passport photo page, and recent passport photographs on white background
Completed visa application forms as required that season, online and on paper
Medical fitness certificate from a registered MBBS doctor, addressing heart health and fitness for altitudes above 4,500 m
PAN card copy, which some agencies and embassies have requested
Proof of residence or employment if requested
Travel insurance policy covering high altitude and evacuation

sections.heading: Age and medical guidance
paras: Age and medical rules are set by the authorities and can be enforced at the visa stage, at the border or both. Treat the figures here as guidance only. The official government yatra has used an age range of 18 to 70, a BMI limit and its own medical tests in Delhi. On the Nepal routes, the age cut-off has been around 70, with medical certificates required and occasional conditional approvals for older pilgrims travelling with a relative. A doctor's fitness check is wise at any age.

Separately from the rules, your own doctor should decide whether the yatra is safe for you. People with heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, chronic lung disease, recent surgery, severe anaemia or pregnancy should not go above 4,500 m.

sections.heading: The process, step by step
paras: A typical sequence in recent seasons has looked like this. Timings are indicative. Book at least three months ahead, and earlier for Saga Dawa or September departures, because the original passport may need to be with the embassy for several weeks.
list: 3–4 months before: choose the route and departure, pay the deposit and send passport scans and photos
2–3 months before: obtain the medical certificate and buy insurance; the agency starts the Tibet permit application
4–6 weeks before: submit the original passport and forms for the group visa as instructed that season, and complete biometrics if required
1–2 weeks before: receive the passport back with the group visa reference, and final documents from the agency
Arrival in Kathmandu or Nepalgunj: final briefing and any document checks
At the border: immigration checks against the group visa list, baggage scanning and health screening

sections.heading: NRIs and OCI cardholders
paras: Indian passport holders living abroad, sometimes called NRIs, have in recent seasons obtained their group visa at the Chinese embassy in Kathmandu after biometrics, and been required to travel in separate groups of at least five with other NRIs or foreign passport holders. They could not join groups of resident Indians, and all members had to enter and leave Tibet together. That makes early coordination essential.

OCI cardholders and people of Indian origin with foreign passports travel under the rules for their passport country, usually with a group visa from Kathmandu. Prices and visa fees then follow their nationality. Ask us which group you fall into before booking.

sections.heading: Practical advice
paras: Ask your agency for the current rules in writing before paying the balance, including the age limit, documents, visa fee and cancellation terms if permits are refused. Keep your travel dates flexible by a day or two at each end, especially on the Simikot route where weather delays are common. Do not carry images or books about the Dalai Lama, maps showing borders China disputes, drones or political literature into Tibet; bags are scanned at every border.
Finally, tell your family that communication will be limited: Indian SIM cards rarely roam in Tibet and many apps are blocked. Your guide carries a phone for emergencies.

faqs.q: Can Indians go to Kailash Mansarovar through Nepal?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian citizens can join private yatras through Nepal via Kyirong, Simikot–Hilsa or Lhasa, on a Chinese group visa and Tibet permits arranged by licensed agencies. The rules for Indian nationals have changed several times since 2023, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where do Indians get the Chinese visa for Kailash yatra?
faqs.a: In recent seasons, resident Indian pilgrims have had their group visa processed through the Chinese embassy in New Delhi, submitting original passports about a month in advance. Non-resident Indians have applied in Kathmandu after biometrics. This has changed before; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the age limit for Kailash yatra for Indians via Nepal?
faqs.a: Around 70 years in recent seasons, expressed for 2026 as a birth year of 1955 or later, with conditional exceptions reported in some years. The official government yatra uses 18–70. These are guidance only and change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is a medical certificate compulsory for Kailash via Nepal?
faqs.a: Yes, a fitness certificate from a registered MBBS doctor has been required in recent seasons, addressing heart health and fitness for altitudes above 4,500 m. Agencies may also check oxygen levels on the way. Get a thorough check-up even if the paperwork seems simple.

faqs.q: Can Indians travel individually to Kailash?
faqs.a: No. Tibet requires pilgrims to travel in groups on a group visa with a licensed Tibetan agency and guide. Individual Indian travellers join an agency's group departure or form a private group with family and friends, subject to minimum sizes set that season.

faqs.q: Can NRIs join a group of Indian residents for Kailash?
faqs.a: In recent seasons, no. Non-resident Indians have had to travel in separate groups of at least five, with other NRIs or foreign passport holders, and enter and leave Tibet together. Check current status before you travel, as grouping rules have changed.

faqs.q: Is the government Kailash yatra cheaper than the Nepal route?
faqs.a: The official yatra's cost is set by the government each year and is often comparable to or lower than overland Nepal-route prices, but it takes about three weeks and depends on selection in a draw. Many pilgrims apply for it and book a Nepal route as a backup.

faqs.q: How early should Indians book Kailash yatra via Nepal?
faqs.a: At least three months ahead, because the original passport may be needed for visa processing weeks before departure and permits are applied for in advance. For Saga Dawa or popular September dates, book four to six months ahead.

faqs.q: What items are not allowed for Indian pilgrims at the Tibet border?
faqs.a: Avoid images or books about the Dalai Lama, maps showing disputed borders, political material and drones. Hindu puja items, idols, rudraksha and personal medicines in original packs with prescriptions are normally fine in personal quantities. Every bag is scanned.
